question.worked_solution:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{8}^{6}={8}^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{2} & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\  & ≡12\cdot 5+4\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\  & ≡12\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{6} & ≡{8}^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\  & ≡4\cdot 4\cdot 4\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\  & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\  & ≡12\cdot 5+4\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\  & ≡12\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{8}^{6}\text{ mod }5=4.
$$
